cells.tense: The spark has caught and you are standing right where it wants finishing.
cells.ask: Finish one thing that's nearly done and hand it off this week. Then begin the next small thing from whatever the ending left open.
cells.core:
Something in you has already lit, and it is not waiting on a plan. The spark caught, and you are the one holding it at the point where it becomes an actual thing. Not the biggest fire in the room — the one that knows how to finish and let go.

What you make tends to land because you do not cling to it. You carry each thing forward by ending it well, and that is the only way anything becomes the next thing. It is rarer than it looks, and it is doing quiet work. The ending is the work, not the reward for it.
cells.sheetLine: You catch the spark, finish it, and hand it on.
cells.verb: catching fire before there is anywhere to point it
cells.place: where a thing is finished and then let go

cells.tense: You are pushing toward the finished version before it has had room to arrive.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you most want to rush and let it sit unfinished for a day. Write down what you actually see in it before you touch it again.
cells.core:
You can see the finished shape and you push everything toward it ahead of its own timing. Projects get hurried to the end because the final picture is already clear, and the hurry is eating the thing it wanted to protect. The next beginning gets no room to breathe.

Wanting the light to prove itself is the pressure you carry. Under the push sits the suspicion that it will not arrive unless you force it, and that bracing is what tires you out. The fire itself is fine. Let one thing stay incomplete and see that it survives the delay.
cells.sheetLine: You're racing a finish line that hasn't arrived.

cells.tense: You started something and you are still standing at that first door.
cells.ask: Say one unfinished thing out loud to someone who can hear it without fixing it, and let the telling be enough for today.
cells.core:
A beginning that is going well here gets to be spoken while it is still rough. The spark is allowed out in front of people before it has a name, and the not-knowing is shared instead of hidden. That is how beginnings get their footing — out loud, imperfect, unfinished in the room.

What is happening now is that the spark stays private and the door stays shut. The energy is there and it isn't reaching anyone, so the thing stays a beginning and doesn't find out what it could be. Nothing has to be figured out first. Let one person be with you in the unfinished part, and don't ask them to complete it for you.
cells.sheetLine: The spark is still there. You've stopped bringing it out.

cells.tense: You are finishing things all day and saying it was just the list getting done.
cells.ask: Name one finished thing out loud and say plainly that you made it. Then say out loud what you want to imagine next.
cells.core:
You land things — the handoff, the launch, the piece that finally came together — and you talk about it like it assembled itself. The making runs fine. The credit for it is the part you keep skipping, and the finished work gets described as still in progress.

The satisfaction is real, sitting just under the habit of shrugging it off. That work is yours, and so is the picture of what comes next. Saying so once, to one person, does not make you a boaster. It gives the credit to the one person who built it and has been quietly taking none.
cells.sheetLine: You finished it. You keep calling it just the work.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that the person's spark is still unshaped rather than merely unspoken — the record gives a threshold state, not a history of what happened there, so Too Little must stay at the door and not narrate the room behind it. A reader could fairly say the finishing is going fine and what's actually missing is direction, which the ask has to leave room for. The ask survives being wrong because it produces a real finished thing either way; the sentence that serves the writer is a clean line about potential igniting, which is why the core keeps the picture plain and lets the undirected spark be the person's, not mine, to name.
